question:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be given by $f(n) = n^2$.

(a) Is $f$ invertible? Justify.

(b) Find the function $g: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ defined by $g(f(n)) = n$ wherever possible.

(c) Can $g$ be a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$? Explain with detailed reasoning regarding the "well-defined" property for inverse functions.

options.A:
(a) $f$ is invertible on $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$.
(b) $g(m)=m^2$.
(c) $g$ is a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ for all natural numbers.
options.B:
(a) $f$ is not one-one, so it is not invertible.
(b) $g(m)=m+1$.
(c) $g$ cannot be defined even on perfect squares.
options.C:
(a) $f$ is one-one but not onto, so it is not invertible as a function $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$.
(b) For perfect squares $m=n^2$, $g(m)=\sqrt m=n$.
(c) $g$ cannot be a function from all of $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ because it is undefined for non-perfect squares such as $2$.
options.D:
(a) $f$ is onto but not one-one.
(b) $g(m)=\frac{1}{m}$.
(c) $g$ is well-defined on all of $\mathbb{N}$.
